passage: The rain was so heavy after school in Nagpur that only one shared auto came, with space for two in the back. Jasleen climbed in and patted the seat next to her, but Mehak, the new girl, slid in first. Sonali had to squeeze in front beside the driver. All the way home she could hear them laughing about the art project they were doing together. Sonali stared at the wet windscreen. Every day this week it had been Mehak, Mehak, Mehak. What if Jasleen didn't need her anymore? When the auto stopped, Jasleen leaned forward. "Sonu, you're coming for the project tomorrow, na?" Sonali's throat was tight. "You have Mehak now." Jasleen blinked. "I have both of you, silly."

qa.q: Who slid into the seat beside Jasleen?
qa.a: Mehak, the new girl.

qa.q: What was Sonali afraid of as she stared at the wet windscreen?
qa.a: She was scared and jealous, fearing Jasleen would like Mehak more and no longer need her.

qa.q: What could Sonali do now that Jasleen has invited her?
qa.a: She could go to the project tomorrow and try to get to know Mehak, and tell Jasleen honestly that she had felt left out.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Sonali's comment "You have Mehak now"?
qa.a: Jasleen seems surprised, since she thinks of both girls as her friends and hadn't noticed Sonali feeling left out.

grounding: In a crowded auto on a rainy day, a girl fears losing her best friend to a new classmate.

passage: Every day after school in Salt Lake, Elizabeth and Rhea walked home together. This week Rhea kept going up to Sharmila's flat instead, because Sharmila had a keyboard and was teaching her songs. On Thursday Elizabeth waited at the gate for ten minutes. Rhea ran past, waving. "Going to Sharmila's!" Elizabeth kicked a stone all the way home. At dinner she pushed her rice around. "Rhea's got a new best friend," she said finally. "Sharmila can play music. I can't do anything like that." Her mother put a hand on hers. "Did Rhea say that?" Elizabeth shook her head slowly.

qa.q: What did Sharmila have that Rhea liked?
qa.a: A keyboard, and she was teaching Rhea songs.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she kicked a stone all the way home?
qa.a: She felt jealous and hurt, worried she was losing Rhea to Sharmila.

qa.q: How could Elizabeth's mother help her with this feeling?
qa.a: She could help Elizabeth ask Rhea directly, or suggest inviting Rhea over for something they both enjoy.

qa.q: How might Rhea see her time at Sharmila's?
qa.a: Rhea may just be excited about the music and not realise that Elizabeth feels left behind.

grounding: A girl fears losing her friend's attention to a peer who teaches music.

passage:
"Dolma, why are you slamming things?"
"I'm not."
Seema Didi raised an eyebrow. "You threw your bag at the wall."
Dolma flopped onto the bed. "Pema sat with the new girl at lunch. Again."
"So?"
"So she's always with Yangchen now. They laugh at jokes I don't even get."
"Did Pema stop talking to you?"
"...No. But she will."
"Ah." Seema sat down. "You're scared you'll lose her."
Dolma hugged her pillow. "Maybe."
"What if you sat with both of them tomorrow?"
"What if they don't want me?"
"What if they do?"

qa.q: What did Dolma throw at the wall?
qa.a: Her bag.

qa.q: What does Dolma's "No. But she will" show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she is jealous and anxious, fearing she will lose Pema even though it hasn't happened yet.

qa.q: What small step did Seema Didi suggest?
qa.a: Sitting with both Pema and Yangchen tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Pema see things if she knew how Dolma felt?
qa.a: Pema might be surprised, since she hasn't stopped talking to Dolma, and could reassure her.

grounding: At home, a girl admits to her older sister that she fears losing her friend to a new girl.

passage:
"Mumma, why can't I have hair like Ritika's?"
Shalini looked up from the vegetables. "Like what?"
"Curly. Bouncy. Everyone says it's so pretty. Mine is just flat."
"Your hair is thick and shiny."
"It's boring! And she has a pink cycle with a bell. And she's good at dancing."
"So you want to be Ritika?"
Aadhya paused. "No... I just want what she has."
"Hmm. What does Ritika say about your drawings?"
Aadhya thought. "She said she wishes she could draw like me."
Shalini smiled. "Interesting."
Aadhya picked at the table, quiet.

qa.q: What colour was Ritika's cycle?
qa.a: Pink, with a bell.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she said "I just want what she has"?
qa.a: She felt envious of Ritika's curly hair, cycle and dancing, wishing she had them too.

qa.q: What worked in Shalini's question about the drawings?
qa.a: It helped Aadhya remember that Ritika admires something in her too, without lecturing her.

qa.q: How might Ritika see Aadhya?
qa.a: Ritika may envy Aadhya's drawing skills, just as Aadhya envies her hair and dancing.

grounding: A girl tells her mother she envies a classmate's hair, cycle and dancing.

passage: I'm Ganga. When I was in Class 4, Wasim sat next to me and could draw anything. Horses, buses, the teacher's face. Everyone crowded around his notebook. I wanted that so badly. I'd go home and try to copy his horses, and they came out like dogs. I stopped showing anyone my drawings and stopped talking to Wasim as much, just because I felt bad around him. One day he asked me to colour one of his pictures because he said I was better with colours. I didn't believe him, but I did it. Now I think I wasted a lot of time wishing I was him.

qa.q: What did Ganga's copied horses look like?
qa.a: They came out like dogs.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel sitting next to Wasim in Class 4?
qa.a: Ganga felt envious and inadequate, wanting Wasim's drawing talent badly.

qa.q: What could Ganga have done differently back then?
qa.a: Ganga could have asked Wasim for tips or enjoyed colouring together instead of pulling away.

qa.q: How might Wasim have seen Ganga pulling away?
qa.a: Wasim might have felt confused or hurt, not knowing why Ganga talked to him less.

grounding: A child looks back on envying a classmate's drawing skill and pulling away from him.

passage: Class 6 note, by Pallavi Nair, class teacher. Aadhya was unusually quiet today. When Ishaani opened her new geometry box with forty colour pencils, Aadhya kept glancing at it. Later she said, loud enough for others, "Rich people get everything." She has an ordinary box and has never complained before. I spoke to her alone at break. She said Ishaani was also always picked for the class play. She looked embarrassed saying it. I told her it's normal to wish for what others have, and asked what she'd like to work on for herself. She said recitation. I've given her the poem for Friday's assembly.

qa.q: How many colour pencils were in Ishaani's new box?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she said "Rich people get everything"?
qa.a: She felt envious of Ishaani's pencils and her place in the class play, and later embarrassed about saying it.

qa.q: What did Pallavi Nair do next to help Aadhya?
qa.a: She spoke to her privately, said wishing is normal, and gave her a recitation poem for assembly.

qa.q: How might Ishaani have felt hearing "Rich people get everything"?
qa.a: Ishaani may have felt hurt or awkward, singled out for her new box.

grounding: A teacher's note records a girl envious of a classmate's belongings and stage roles, and how she helped.

passage: Chetan had joined the Chembur cricket team only two weeks ago. On Sunday the match was stopped by rain after one over. The boys crowded under a tin shed, wet and cold. Chetan stood at the edge, not sure where to go. Then Vidya, the captain, shouted, "Oi, new guy, get in here!" and pulled him into the middle. They started the team chant, and someone thumped his back. Chetan didn't know all the words yet, but he shouted anyway. For the first time since moving, he felt warm, even though his shirt was soaked. "Same time next week?" Vidya asked. "Definitely," Chetan said.

qa.q: How long had Chetan been on the team?
qa.a: Only two weeks.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he shouted the chant?
qa.a: He felt accepted and happy, warm inside for the first time since moving.

qa.q: What did Vidya do that helped Chetan feel he belonged?
qa.a: Vidya called him into the middle of the group, drawing him into the chant.

qa.q: How might the team captain see Chetan by the end?
qa.a: Vidya likely sees him as part of the team now, happy he joined the chant.

grounding: A new boy under a shed in the rain feels he truly belongs when the cricket team pulls him into their chant.

passage: In the Powai colony, the boys with cycles rode round the park every evening. Saurabh had watched for months from his balcony. When he finally got a second-hand cycle, he rode slowly near the gate. Francis, the oldest, circled back. "You're the one on the fourth floor, right? Come." By the third round they were calling him "Speedy," because he'd almost crashed into a bench. Saurabh laughed louder than anyone. At home he couldn't stop talking about it. "They gave me a name, Mummy. A real one." He went to bed smiling.

qa.q: What did the boys start calling Saurabh?
qa.a: "Speedy."

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel about getting a nickname?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and accepted, as though he was truly part of the group.

qa.q: What could Saurabh's mother say to support him?
qa.a: She could share his happiness and ask about the new friends, while encouraging him to keep his other friendships too.

qa.q: How might Francis see the new boy?
qa.a: Francis likely sees Saurabh as a friendly addition and enjoys welcoming him.

grounding: A boy finds deep happiness in being accepted and nicknamed by a colony cycle group.

passage:
"Harish Bhaiya! Guess what!"
"You found a kitten?"
"No! The dance group asked me to join. For the annual day!"
"The same group that didn't pick you last year?"
"Yes! Kritika said they need me for the front row. And they saved me a seat at lunch." Yamini spun round. "They all have matching hair clips, and they said they'll get me one."
"You're really happy, huh?"
"I don't feel like an outsider anymore." She stopped. "Do you think they'll still want me if I mess up the steps?"
Harish smiled. "They picked you. Practise, and ask them for help."

qa.q: What did the group say they would get Yamini?
qa.a: A matching hair clip.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she said, "I don't feel like an outsider anymore"?
qa.a: She felt happy and secure, with a deep sense of belonging, though also a little worried about messing up.

qa.q: What did Harish advise Yamini to do?
qa.a: To practise and ask the group for help.

qa.q: How might Harish see his sister's excitement?
qa.a: Harish seems pleased for her, remembering she wasn't picked last year.

grounding: A girl tells her brother how accepted she feels after being invited into a dance group.

passage: In the Pune school, the maths test results were read out. Afreen, 20 out of 20. Aditi, 13. Aditi looked at her desk. On the way home, Afreen chattered about the drawing competition she'd also won. Aditi said nothing. At home she threw her bag down. "I'm the dumbest one," she told her father. "Afreen is good at everything." Her father sat beside her. "Last month you got 9." "But Afreen got 20!" "And you got four more than you did last month." Aditi sniffed. "It still feels small."

qa.q: What did Aditi get on the maths test?
qa.a: 13 out of 20.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she said "I'm the dumbest one"?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and ashamed, comparing herself to Afreen's perfect score.

qa.q: How could her father continue to help Aditi?
qa.a: He could keep pointing to her own progress and help her set a small goal for the next test.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the walk home?
qa.a: Afreen probably didn't notice Aditi was upset, since she was excited about her own wins.

grounding: A girl feels inferior when comparing her maths marks to a friend's perfect score.

passage:
"Deepika, come in! The water's warm!"
"No, I'm fine here."
Devika swam over. "You haven't gone past the rope all summer."
"Everyone else can swim to the other side."
"So can you. Almost."
"I can't. I just splash. You swim like a fish, and even little Riya's faster than me."
"Riya's been going since she was five."
"I'm eleven and I still can't." Deepika wrapped her towel tighter. "Everyone's watching me."
"Nobody's watching. Look, they're all racing."
Deepika glanced up. "Maybe."
"Come to the rope with me. Just the rope."
Deepika hesitated, then stood. "Just the rope."

qa.q: Who swims "like a fish"?
qa.a: Devika.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she wrapped her towel tighter?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and self-conscious, sure everyone was watching her.

qa.q: What small step did Devika suggest?
qa.a: Swimming just to the rope together.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had teased her about not swimming?
qa.a: Deepika would likely feel worse and stay out of the water.

grounding: A girl feels inadequate about her swimming compared with her cousin and others.

passage: I'm Kishore. Last year Indu joined our class from Delhi. The first week, Ma'am asked her to read aloud and she read the English lesson smoothly, like a newsreader. Then it was my turn. I stumbled on "enormous" and "whispered." Someone giggled. My ears went hot. After that, I kept comparing. Indu's handwriting, Indu's answers, Indu's shoes. I felt small all the time. One day Indu asked me to explain a Marathi poem she didn't understand. I did, easily. She said, "You're so good at this." I didn't know what to say.

qa.q: Which words did Kishore stumble on?
qa.a: "Enormous" and "whispered."

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after comparing everything to Indu?
qa.a: Kishore felt small and inadequate all the time.

qa.q: What could Kishore learn from explaining the Marathi poem?
qa.a: That everyone has different strengths, and Kishore has some that Indu admires.

qa.q: How might Indu have seen Kishore during that time?
qa.a: Indu likely saw Kishore as good at Marathi and may not have known Kishore felt small.

grounding: A child looks back on feeling inferior after comparing to a new classmate's English reading.

passage:
"She stepped over the line! Did you see? She stepped over!"
"Jasleen, calm down."
"No, Hafsa! Neha stepped over and still tagged me. It's cheating!"
"The umpire didn't see."
"That's not fair! Rules are rules!" Jasleen's face was red. "If I did that, they'd call me out."
Hafsa put a hand on her arm. "I saw it too."
"Then say something!"
"Okay. But not shouting. Let's tell Neha after the round."
Jasleen breathed hard. "Fine. But she has to say it."
"She will. Come."

qa.q: Who stepped over the line?
qa.a: Neha.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when her face went red?
qa.a: She felt indignant and angry at what she saw as cheating.

qa.q: What did Hafsa suggest, and why could it work better?
qa.a: She suggested talking to Neha calmly after the round, which may get a fair result without a shouting match.

qa.q: How might Neha feel if Jasleen confronts her by shouting?
qa.a: Neha might become defensive and deny it rather than admit the mistake.

grounding: A girl burns with indignation at a player breaking the rules in a game, and a friend helps her channel it.

passage: I'm Sangeeta. In Class 5, there was one water tap for the whole floor, and we all lined up at break. Ujjwal always pushed to the front. One hot day, I'd waited ten minutes, and he walked right past everyone and filled his bottle. I got so angry my hands shook. I shouted, "That's cheating! Back of the line!" Everyone turned. Ujjwal went red and stepped back. Later I felt a bit shaky about shouting, but I still think it was unfair. Now I'd probably say it more calmly, but I'd still say it.

qa.q: How long had Sangeeta waited at the tap?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Ujjwal walked past everyone?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt indignant and furious, so angry that Sangeeta's hands shook.

qa.q: Looking back, what would Sangeeta do differently?
qa.a: Say it more calmly, but still speak up against the unfairness.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt when everyone turned to look?
qa.a: Ujjwal likely felt embarrassed and ashamed, going red and stepping back.

grounding: A child recalls feeling angry at a classmate cutting the queue and speaking up.

passage: Coach's note, under-12 kabaddi, Thursday. Yamini Rao. In the practice match, Sonali shouted at the other team's raider that he had crossed the bonus line without touching, and that the point shouldn't count. She was loud and pointed at him, and her voice cracked. I stopped the game. She was right about the line, and I said so. But I also told her that shouting at a player won't change a call; she can raise her hand and tell me. She nodded, still breathing hard. After the match she came to me and asked to learn the full rules. I've given her the rule sheet to read.

qa.q: What did Sonali say the raider had done?
qa.a: Crossed the bonus line without touching.

qa.q: What does Sonali's voice cracking suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt strongly indignant, upset by what she saw as unfair.

qa.q: What did Yamini Rao do after the match?
qa.a: She gave Sonali the full rule sheet to read after Sonali asked to learn the rules.

qa.q: How might the raider have felt when Sonali shouted at him?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed or defensive at being called out so loudly.

grounding: A coach's note on a girl who reacts hotly to a rule being broken in kabaddi, and how the coach responds.

passage: Lakshmi Ammamma settled in her chair. "Urmila, when I was ten, we had no books at home. Our neighbour, Venkatesh Mama, was a clerk and had shelves full. One day he saw me reading an old newspaper on the step. The next Sunday he knocked and handed me a book. 'Return it next week, and I'll give you another.' He did that for two whole years. I didn't have words then for how thankful I was. I just made him a card from a matchbox and drew a book on it. He kept it on his shelf till he died." Urmila touched the old matchbox on the table. "Is this it?" "His son returned it to me."

qa.q: What did young Lakshmi make for Venkatesh Mama?
qa.a: A card from a matchbox with a book drawn on it.

qa.q: How did young Lakshmi feel about Venkatesh Mama's books?
qa.a: She felt deeply thankful and grateful, even without words for it.

qa.q: What was the key moment in the story, and how did young Lakshmi show her thanks?
qa.a: The key moment was the neighbour noticing her reading and bringing her books; she showed thanks with a handmade card.

qa.q: How might Venkatesh Mama have felt about keeping the card?
qa.a: He likely felt touched and appreciated, which is why he kept it for so long.

grounding: A grandmother remembers her gratitude to a neighbour who lent her books as a child.

passage: It was exam day, pouring rain, and Tushar had left his lunch box and his pen at home. He stood at his desk, wet and panicking. Raghav, beside him, silently held out a blue pen. Then, at break, he pushed half his idli across. "I'm not that hungry," he said. But Tushar saw him look at the idli before giving it. Tushar's throat felt tight. After the exam, he found Raghav at the gate. "Thanks, yaar. You didn't have to." Raghav shrugged. "You'd do it." Tushar decided he'd bring extra snacks tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Raghav hold out to Tushar?
qa.a: A blue pen.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he saw Raghav look at the idli before giving it?
qa.a: He felt grateful and touched, understanding that Raghav had given up something he wanted.

qa.q: How did Tushar plan to show his thanks?
qa.a: By bringing extra snacks the next day.

qa.q: How might Raghav see his own kindness?
qa.a: Raghav seems to think of it as normal, something Tushar would also do.

grounding: On a rainy exam day, a boy feels grateful when a classmate shares his pen and lunch.

passage: Karthik broke his wrist falling off his cycle in Kochi and missed a week of school. When he came back, his arm in a cast, Mohit handed him a thick notebook. "I copied all the notes. Science, social studies, maths. Twice, so one's in neat writing." Karthik flipped through. Mohit had even drawn the diagrams. "You did this every night?" "Mostly." Karthik felt a warm lump in his chest. He knew Mohit hated writing. "Thanks. Really." Mohit grinned. "Just don't make me copy the next test."

qa.q: How long did Karthik miss school?
qa.a: A week.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he felt a warm lump in his chest?
qa.a: He felt grateful and moved, knowing Mohit hated writing and had done it for him anyway.

qa.q: How could Karthik return the kindness?
qa.a: He could thank Mohit properly, perhaps help him with a subject he finds hard, or be there when Mohit needs help.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel about his effort being noticed?
qa.a: He likely feels happy and a bit shy, making a joke to cover it.

grounding: A boy feels grateful when a friend copies a week of notes for him after his injury.

passage: Pradeep Chacha leaned back. "Akash, when I was eleven, our colony had a rule for cricket: whoever breaks a window owns up. No running. One day my shot went straight through Mrs Kulkarni's glass. The others shouted, 'Run!' but I walked up and rang her bell. My knees were shaking. She was angry, but she said, 'At least you came.' When I walked back to the others, they looked at me differently. Next day, Bunty said, 'You kept the rule, man.' I felt taller that whole week, like I was the kind of person who does the right thing." Akash grinned. "Did you pay for it?" "Six months of pocket money."

qa.q: Whose window did young Pradeep break?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni's.

qa.q: How did young Pradeep feel when Bunty said "You kept the rule, man"?
qa.a: He felt proud and validated, like someone who does the right thing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what could young Pradeep have done if he felt too scared to go alone?
qa.a: The turning point was choosing to ring her bell instead of running; he could have asked a friend to come with him.

qa.q: How might Mrs Kulkarni have seen young Pradeep?
qa.a: She was angry about the window, but respected that he came to own up.

grounding: An uncle recalls feeling proud and validated after following the colony rule to own up to a broken window.

passage: Ten minutes left in the Class 7 test, and Bhavna Ma'am stepped out to answer the phone. The room buzzed. Someone whispered answers across the aisle. Anand kept his eyes on his paper, though his last answer was blank. "Psst, Anand, number 5?" "We said no talking in tests," Anand whispered back. "Everyone agreed." He felt his heart thumping. When Bhavna Ma'am returned, she looked around. "Who kept the rule?" A few raised hands, Anand's among them. "Thank you," she said. Anand sat straighter. His blank answer still bothered him, but he felt good.

qa.q: How many minutes were left in the test?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Bhavna Ma'am said "Thank you"?
qa.a: He felt proud and validated for keeping the rule, even with a blank answer.

qa.q: What could Bhavna Ma'am do to keep the class's agreement strong?
qa.a: She could remind everyone why they agreed on the rule and not leave the room during tests.

qa.q: How might the classmate who whispered see Anand's reply?
qa.a: They might feel annoyed or a little embarrassed at being reminded of the rule.

grounding: During a test, a boy keeps the agreed no-talking rule and feels validated when the teacher thanks those who did.

passage: In the Thane society, Sunday was waste-sorting day, and Irawati was proud of her job: checking the bins in their wing. Wet waste in green, dry in blue. When Kamal Uncle from the third floor tossed a plastic bag into the green bin, she said, "Uncle, that goes in blue. We all agreed at the meeting." He paused, then moved it. "Right you are." Irawati felt a glow. Then she saw her own brother drop a wrapper in green. "Arre! Even you?" Her mother laughed. "Rules for everyone, na?" Irawati moved the wrapper herself, smiling.

qa.q: What colour bin was for wet waste?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling after Kamal Uncle moved the bag?
qa.a: She felt proud and validated, a glow of doing the right thing.

qa.q: How could Irawati make sure her reminders come across kindly?
qa.a: She could keep her tone friendly and help fix mistakes, as she did with her brother's wrapper.

qa.q: How might Kamal Uncle see being corrected by a child?
qa.a: He seems a little surprised but takes it well, agreeing that she's right.

grounding: A girl feels proud upholding her building's waste-sorting rule, even with her own family.

passage: In Enugu, Chidi got 4 out of 20 on the spelling test. He hid the paper in his bag and didn't eat dinner. His older sister Ada found it. "Four," she said. "What now?" Chidi shrugged, eyes wet. "I'm bad at spelling." "Or you haven't practised." She made him a list of ten words. Every evening for two weeks, he wrote them on the back door with chalk and she tested him. Some nights he wanted to quit. The next test, he got 14. He ran home waving it. "Not twenty yet," he said. "But next time."

qa.q: What score did Chidi get on the first test?
qa.a: 4 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Chidi feel after hiding the test?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and discouraged, believing he was bad at spelling.

qa.q: What helped Chidi improve?
qa.a: Practising every evening for two weeks with Ada testing him.

qa.q: How might Ada see her brother's new score?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and happy that his effort paid off. 🎉

grounding: A boy recovers from a poor spelling score through steady practice with his sister's help.

passage: At the district sports club, Rukmini lost her badminton match 21–8. She sat on the bench with her towel over her head. Coach Salma sat beside her. "What happened?" "I'm terrible at serves. Everyone saw." "True, your serves were weak today." Rukmini's shoulders dropped. "So what's one thing you want to fix?" A long pause. "Serves." "Then come tomorrow at six, before the others." The next morning Rukmini was there at quarter to six, racket in hand, practising serve after serve into the corner. Salma watched, nodding.

qa.q: What was the match score?
What does Rukmini putting her towel over her head suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt embarrassed and discouraged after losing so badly.

qa.q: What did Coach Salma do that helped Rukmini bounce back?
qa.a: She was honest about the serves and helped Rukmini choose one thing to fix and a time to practise.

qa.q: How might Coach Salma feel seeing Rukmini arrive early?
qa.a: She would likely feel encouraged and pleased by Rukmini's determination.

grounding: A girl bounces back after a heavy badminton loss by choosing one skill to practise.

passage: I'm Jaya, Aparna's sister. When Aparna got her maths test back with 11 out of 40, she didn't cry. She just went very quiet and sat on the stairs for a long time. The next day she made a chart and stuck it on the fridge: "30 minutes maths every evening." At first I thought she'd give up by Sunday. But for a whole month, every evening after snacks, she sat at the table with her book. Some days she slammed it shut and stomped around, then came back. On the next test she got 26. She didn't say much, but she smiled all evening.

qa.q: What did Aparna write on the chart?
qa.a: "30 minutes maths every evening."

qa.q: What might Aparna have been feeling when she sat quietly on the stairs?
qa.a: She probably felt disappointed and upset after the low score.

qa.q: What worked in how Aparna recovered?
qa.a: She set a small, steady daily routine and kept coming back even when frustrated.

qa.q: How does Jaya's view of her sister change?
qa.a: Jaya expected Aparna to give up but is impressed by her steady effort and improvement.

grounding: A sister observes a girl bounce back from a poor maths score through daily practice.

passage: The power had gone out in the Bhopal flat, and the fan stopped. Imran, nine, was bored and sweaty. Rehana Aapa lit a candle. "Riddle. What has hands but can't clap?" Imran thought. "A... monkey with no arms?" "A clock!" He groaned. "Another." "Why did the tomato turn red?" "Because it was hot?" "Because it saw the salad dressing!" Imran stared, then burst out laughing. "Dressing! Like putting on clothes!" He laughed so much the candle flickered. "My turn," he said. "Why was the fan sad?" Rehana waited. "Because nobody's a fan of it in a power cut!"

qa.q: What was the answer to "What has hands but can't clap?"
qa.a: A clock.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he burst out laughing at the tomato joke?
qa.a: He felt delighted and amused as he suddenly understood the double meaning of "dressing."

qa.q: How could Rehana keep building on Imran's love of wordplay?
qa.a: She could keep swapping riddles and puns with him and help him invent more of his own.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel about Imran's fan joke?
qa.a: She might feel proud and amused that he made his own pun.

grounding: During a power cut, a boy starts understanding puns and makes one of his own.

passage: In the Lucknow kitchen, Rajni burned the toast again. Her older cousin Vandana walked in, sniffed and said, "Wow. The famous chef strikes again." Rajni's face fell. Then she saw Vandana was grinning and already reaching for the butter. "Very funny," Rajni said, trying not to smile. "It's charcoal toast, very healthy." Vandana laughed. "Five stars." Rajni laughed too. She knew Vandana wasn't being mean; she teased like this with everyone she liked. They scraped the black bits off together.

qa.q: What did Vandana call Rajni?
qa.a: "The famous chef."

qa.q: How did Rajni's feelings change after she saw Vandana grinning?
qa.a: At first she felt hurt, then relieved and amused once she realised it was friendly teasing.

qa.q: What helped Rajni read the teasing correctly?
qa.a: Noticing Vandana's grin and remembering that she teases people she likes.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had said it with a frown and walked away?
qa.a: The same words might have felt mean, and Rajni could have taken it as an insult.

grounding: A girl reads her cousin's sarcastic joke about burnt toast as friendly teasing rather than meanness.

passage:
"Parveen, why did the maths book look so sad?"
"Why?"
"Because it had too many problems!"
Parveen rolled her eyes but smiled. "That's so old."
Bhavna grinned. "Okay, okay. What do you call a sleeping bull?"
"What?"
"A bulldozer!"
Parveen laughed. "Okay, that's good."
"And your drawing today? A real masterpiece. Museums will fight over it."
Parveen's smile dropped. "You think it's bad?"
"No! I'm joking. It was nice. The cat was cute."
"Oh." Parveen relaxed. "Then they can fight. I'm not selling."
"Exactly!"

qa.q: What do you call a sleeping bull, according to Bhavna?
qa.a: A bulldozer.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when her smile dropped?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unsure, thinking Bhavna was mocking her drawing.

qa.q: What helped clear up the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Bhavna quickly explained she was joking and said something kind about the cat.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when Parveen's smile dropped?
qa.a: Bhavna likely felt worried and sorry that her tease had landed wrong.

grounding: Two girls trade puns, and one briefly misreads a tease as meanness before understanding it.

passage: Zubin lent Pradeep his cycle on Saturday morning in the Chandigarh colony. "Back by six," Zubin said. "I need it for tuition." At half past five, Pradeep was still racing round the park with the others. "One more round!" someone shouted. Pradeep looked at the sky. "No, I promised Zubin." He rode back and handed it over at ten to six. Zubin smiled. "You're on time." "You trusted me," Pradeep said. "Next time I'll lend you my skates." Zubin grinned. "Deal."

qa.q: By what time did Zubin want the cycle back?
qa.a: By six.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he decided to go back?
qa.a: He felt torn: tempted to keep playing, but uneasy about breaking his promise to Zubin.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Returning the cycle on time, because it kept Zubin's trust and led to more sharing.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Pradeep after this?
qa.a: Zubin likely trusts him more and is happy to share again.

grounding: A boy returns a borrowed cycle on time because he values trust and reciprocity.

passage:
"It's my turn to choose the show," said Rashmi.
"No, you chose yesterday," Darshan said.
"But you got the last samosa."
"That's not the same thing!"
Rashmi crossed her arms. "Fine. What's fair?"
Darshan thought. "We made a rule: Monday me, Tuesday you, and so on."
"Today's Wednesday."
"So it's me."
Rashmi scowled, then sighed. "Okay. But tomorrow I choose, no matter what."
"Deal. And you can have the next samosa."
Rashmi laughed. "Now that's fair."

qa.q: What day was it?
qa.a: Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she scowled and then sighed?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at first, then accepting, because the rule they made was fair.

qa.q: What helped them settle the argument?
qa.a: Remembering the rule they had agreed on and offering something back.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Rashmi's final agreement?
qa.a: He likely feels relieved and respected that she kept to the rule.

grounding: A brother and sister settle a TV argument by relying on their agreed turn-taking rule.

passage: I'm Jahnavi. Our Class 6 has an honour shelf of storybooks. There's no teacher watching; you write your name in the register and bring the book back in a week. Last month I took a mystery and forgot it at Nani's. Harsha asked, "Where's the book? I'm next." My stomach dropped. I made Papa drive to Nani's that evening to get it, and returned it the next day. I realised the shelf only works if everyone brings books back. If people stop, then no one trusts anyone. Now I set a reminder on the fridge.

qa.q: How long do students have to return a book?
qa.a: A week.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when Harsha asked where the book was?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt guilty and worried, with a stomach that dropped.

qa.q: What could help Jahnavi return books on time in future?
qa.a: Jahnavi now sets a reminder on the fridge, which is a simple way to remember.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Jahnavi's effort to get the book back?
qa.a: Harsha likely feels respected and trusts Jahnavi to keep to the shelf rules.

grounding: A child reflects on why the class honour shelf depends on everyone returning books.
